To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hemodynamic response varies across subjects and brain areas, and that these variations can affect the statistical analyses used to determine whether or not a brain region is active.
(1) the HRF is variable across subjects and brain areas, (2) the variability is greater across subjects than across brain areas, and (3) the variability affects statistical analysis of fMRI data.

1) the hemodynamic response varies across subjects and brain areas; 2) this variation can cause false negatives; 3) this variation can affect parameter estimation and therefore the results of random-effects analyses; and 4) experiment design and statistical analysis methods can limit the effects of variation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the variability of HRFs in fMRI and its effect on the results of statistical analysis.
the variability of hemodynamic response function (HRF) estimates across brain regions and individuals, and its effects on statistical analyses using the General Linear Model (GLM) in fMRI studies.
the effect of HRF variation across subjects and brain areas on the detection of activity using the GLM.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of an empirically derived, rather than a canonical, HRF is advisable, and the use of a derivative is not always helpful.
HRFs vary, but that this variation is small enough so that the use of a canonical HRF in a GLM is acceptable in most cases.
HRF variation is not an issue for the majority of studies but that it can be for some studies and that the potential for problems can be reduced by careful design of the study and analysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of HRF variation can be mitigated by using the most appropriate experimental design and analysis model, but the effects are not completely eliminated.
the HRF is a very important component in fMRI analysis.
the effects of HRF variation can be minimized by (1) using a rapid event-related experimental design, and (2) including the HRF derivative as an additional regressor in the GLM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HRF can vary significantly across subjects and brain areas.

researchers should be careful in their assumptions about how HRFs vary and that the effects of these variations on statistical analyses can be minimized by using a rapid sampling rate and by including the first derivative of an HRF in the general linear model.
HRFs vary significantly across brain regions and subjects and that these variations can lead to false positives and/or false negatives, depending on the experimental design and analysis method.
